core.text: The subjunctive can also soften a statement into a possibility: **the potential subjunctive (the 'could / would / may' form: velim = I would like)**. *Tē adiuvem* — I could help you; *aliquis dīcat* — someone might say; *fortasse veniam* — I may come. Its commonest use is polite: *velim* — I would like; *nōlim* — I would rather not; *mālim* — I would prefer. Latin name: *coniūnctīvus potentiālis*.
English does the same with *would*, *could*, *might*: *I would like to come*, *one might say*.
Present (or perfect) subjunctive in a main clause, often with aliquis, quis or fortasse: 'could / would / may'. Negative nōn.

invented.en: I would like to come, but I can't.
Someone might say: 'I don't believe it.'

core.text: Same form, different tone: **the subjunctive as a wish or gentle command (eamus = let's go; veniat = let him come)** wants something to happen (*veniat* — let him come); the potential only says it could (*veniat* — he may come). Wishes take *nē*, possibilities *nōn*; *fortasse* or *aliquis* points to the potential.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 27) call it possibility or probability, 'often used merely to weaken a statement in order to be polite', and single out *possim, velim, nōlim, mālim*: *venīre possim* — I could come; *venīre velim* — I would like to come.

With the imperfect subjunctive the possibility moves into the past or becomes unreal: *vellem* — I would wish (but it cannot be); *dīcerēs* — you would have said. The perfect subjunctive is common in cautious statements: *haud sciō an ita dīxerim* — I rather think I said so. In the second person it is the general 'you': *crēdās* — one would believe.

teach.title: A verb that only says 'could'
teach.say: The same present subjunctive can let go of its force entirely and say only that something is possible. That is **the potential subjunctive (the 'could / would / may' form: velim = I would like)**. *Tē iuvāre possim* is not 'let me help you' but 'I could help you'; *possīs* is 'you could'. Nothing has been wished for and nobody has been told anything: the speaker is holding the idea out at arm's length.

check.ask: Does possīs say that you can do it, or that you could?

teach.title: velim and nōlim: the polite ones
teach.say: The commonest potentials by far are the little verbs of wanting: **velim** 'I would like', **nōlim** 'I would rather not'. They are the present subjunctive of *volō* and *nōlō*, and Latin reaches for them exactly where English softens 'I want' into 'I would like'. The ending is the ordinary **-m** of the 'I' person, on the subjunctive stem (what is left of the verb before the ending) *veli-* / *nōli-*.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of volō that means 'I would like'.

teach.title: The words that point at it
teach.say: Latin usually sets a word beside the verb that points at the possibility: *fortasse* 'perhaps', *aliquis* 'someone', *nēmō* 'nobody' — and a question with *quis* 'who': *Quis haec verba vēra esse crēdat?* is 'who would believe these words are true?', not 'who believes them?'. *Aliquis dīcat* is 'someone might say' — an imagined speaker, not one who has spoken. When one of these stands next to a subjunctive in a main clause (the sentence's own verb, not one tucked inside another clause), read 'could', 'might' or 'would'.

teach.title: The negative is nōn
teach.say: This is the test that separates the two main-clause uses. A wish or command is denied with *nē*; a possibility is denied with **nōn**: *nōn crēdās*, 'you would not believe'. So *nē crēdās* forbids you to believe, while *nōn crēdās* only doubts — the same verb in the same person, and the negative is the whole difference. Look at which negative is standing there before you decide which reading the sentence wants.

check.ask: What is crēdat doing here — wishing for it, or saying it could happen?

teach.title: Using it in any person
teach.say: The potential is not only for 'I'. *intellegās* 'you could understand', *emat* 'he would buy', *ferat* 'he could carry' — the endings are the ordinary present subjunctive ones you already know, and the sense stays 'could / would'. Put the right person on the subjunctive stem (what is left of the verb before the ending) and let the rest of the sentence do the softening.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of volō that means 'would want'.
